title: Heat-mortality relations fitted on 2000-2014 deaths improved 2015-2024 summer death forecasts in 114 European regions, but the heat response was 14% below stationary expectation
abstract: Question: is a summer heat-mortality relation operationally forecastable, and which campaign rule identifies it: the response-class rule (disease and population responses: use a trailing mean) or the training-only false-signal gate? Approach: we froze and timestamped a plan, then fitted per-region relations (weekly log deaths with year and week effects and a temperature hinge for the week and the previous week) on Eurostat weekly deaths and E-OBS v32.0e temperature. Cohort A: 114 NUTS 2 regions in 18 countries, training summers 2000-2014, test summers 2015-2019 and 2022-2024 (ISO weeks 23-35). Cohort B: 94 regions in 10 countries, training to 2019, test 2022-2024. Forecasts used observed weather. Results: a trailing level plus the frozen heat term beat the temperature-blind trailing mean (median skill 0.18, 95% country-bootstrap interval 0.08 to 0.25; hot weeks 0.59; cohort B 0.11). No shifted-climate null reached the training signal (false-signal rate 0.00), so the gate chose climate correctly and the class rule did not. Training R2_cv ranked regional skill (rho 0.58). The calibration slope of the frozen heat term fell from 0.92 in held-out training summers (stationary expectation with estimation noise) to 0.79 in test summers (difference -0.13, interval -0.21 to -0.04). The decline was in warm and southern regions (-0.21) and absent in cool ones; 2022 was an exception (slope 1.01; COVID overlap). Cohort B showed no detectable change (-0.07, -0.20 to 0.14). Limitations: observed weather, all-cause all-age deaths, area-weighted exposure, no France, Germany, Italy or UK in cohort A, and no test of the causes of the decline.
